plan: Eight new items (equivocal WIC, ant step-counting evidence, sampling-flaw inference, intervening-clause agreement, colon before an explanation, exception transition, similarity synthesis, overall structure) plus S019-04 and S019-06 relabelled easy.

passages.title: An open answer
passages.text: The ambassador's reply to the proposal was deliberately ______: it could be read either as acceptance or as refusal, which left both governments room to keep negotiating.

passages.title: Counting steps
passages.text: Researchers hypothesized that desert ants find their way back to the nest partly by keeping track of the number of steps they have taken. To test this, they lengthened the legs of some ants with tiny stilts and shortened the legs of others after the ants had walked from the nest to a food source.

passages.title: Gym survey
passages.text: A survey of the members of a large gym found that 80 percent of them exercise at least four times a week. A city official cited this result as evidence that most of the city's residents exercise frequently. However, ______

passages.title: Sailors' letters
passages.text: The archive, which holds thousands of letters written by sailors to their families over two centuries, ______ open to researchers by appointment on weekdays.

passages.title: Coating results
passages.text: The engineers tested a new coating on steel panels left outdoors near the ocean for a year. The results were ______ panels with the coating showed about half as much rust as uncoated panels.

passages.title: Day-flying bats
passages.text: Most bats hunt at night, which lets them avoid hawks and other daytime predators. ______ a few species, such as some fruit bats on islands with no large predatory birds, regularly fly and feed during the day.

passages.title: Late debut
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Penelope Fitzgerald published her first novel in 1977, at age 60.
• She won the Booker Prize two years later for Offshore.
• Laura Ingalls Wilder published her first novel, Little House in the Big Woods, in 1932, at age 65.
• Wilder's Little House books became classics of children's literature.

passages.title: A revised date
passages.text: For decades, archaeologists dated a hilltop fort to about 500 BCE, relying on the style of pottery found inside its walls. Recently, a team used radiocarbon dating on charcoal from the fort's earliest hearths and obtained dates near 800 BCE. The team argues that the pottery style must have remained in use for far longer than previously assumed.

passages.title: A town's decline (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
A historian argues that the plague of 1349 caused the decline of the market town of Hollin, which lost much of its population and trade in the years that followed.

Text 2
Tax records from Hollin show that the number of households paying the market tax fell steadily from about 1310 onward, as trade shifted to a new port downriver. The plague then sharply reduced a population that was already shrinking.

passages.title: Ferry fares
passages.text:
After a ferry company cut its fares, it compared average daily ridership before and after the cut.
Season | Riders before cut | Riders after cut
Summer | 4,000 | 4,400
Winter | 1,000 | 1,300
A company analyst claims that, in percentage terms, the fare cut increased ridership more in winter than in summer.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: it could be read either as acceptance or as refusal
candidates.explanation: A reply that can be read two opposite ways is "equivocal."

B.rationale: "Candid" means frank and direct; a reply open to two readings is not direct.

C.rationale: "Belligerent" means hostile; nothing suggests hostility, and the reply kept negotiations open.

D.rationale: "Verbose" means wordy; the text concerns the reply's double meaning, not its length.

hints: What does it mean that the reply could be read two ways?
candidates.remember: Match the word to the description that follows the colon.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (support a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.A: Ants on stilts and ants with shortened legs both returned directly to the nest without error.
choices.B: Ants with shortened legs carried smaller pieces of food back to the nest than the ants on stilts did.
choices.C: Ants on stilts overshot the nest on the way back, and ants with shortened legs stopped short of it.
choices.D: Ants on stilts walked more slowly on the return trip to the nest than they had on the way out.

candidates.evidence: keeping track of the number of steps they have taken
candidates.explanation: If ants count steps, longer strides carry them farther than the counted distance (overshooting) and shorter strides fall short. C describes exactly that pattern.

A.rationale: If the ants returned correctly regardless of stride length, step counting would not explain their navigation.

B.rationale: The size of the food carried says nothing about how the ants judged distance.

D.rationale: Walking speed does not show whether the ants counted steps to judge distance.

hints: If an ant counts steps, what happens when each step gets longer?

strategy.explanation: Predict the result step counting would produce, then match.

candidates.remember: Supporting evidence is the result the hypothesis predicts.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the survey found that some gym members exercise fewer than four times a week.
choices.B: the gym is one of the largest in the city and has members of many ages.
choices.C: frequent exercise has been shown to improve health in many studies.
choices.D: gym members are likely to exercise more often than city residents in general.

candidates.evidence: A city official cited this result as evidence that most of the city's residents exercise frequently.
candidates.explanation: "However" signals a flaw in the official's reasoning. Gym members are not a representative sample of residents: they are probably more active than average.

A.rationale: That 20 percent exercise less does not undermine the official's conclusion about residents.

B.rationale: Size and age variety do not fix the problem that all respondents chose to join a gym.

C.rationale: This is about the benefits of exercise, not about whether the survey represents residents.

hints: Who was surveyed, and who is the conclusion about?

strategy.explanation: Compare the sample with the group in the conclusion.

candidates.remember: A conclusion about a group needs a sample that represents that group.

author_checklist.hardness: The flaw is not stated; the student must notice that the sample (gym members) differs from the target group (all residents). Choice B looks like a reassurance about the sample and catches quick readers.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The archive, which holds thousands of letters
candidates.explanation: The subject "archive" is singular, and the sentence needs a finite verb: "is."

A.rationale: The subject is "archive," which is singular; "letters" and "families" are inside the clause.

C.rationale: "Being" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

D.rationale: "To be" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

hints: Read the sentence without the part between the commas.

strategy.explanation: Remove the "which" clause and read the sentence again.

candidates.remember: Skip the clause between commas to find the subject.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: panels with the coating showed about half as much rust
candidates.explanation: The second clause explains what made the results clear, and a colon after an independent clause can introduce such an explanation.

B.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

C.rationale: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: A semicolon followed by "and" is not standard between these clauses.

hints: Is the text before the blank a complete sentence? Does what follows explain it?
candidates.remember: A colon can introduce an explanation after a complete sentence.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The second sentence presents an exception to the general pattern in the first, so a contrasting transition, "Nevertheless," fits.

A.rationale: Daytime flying is not a result of avoiding daytime predators; it departs from that pattern.

B.rationale: The day-flying bats are not an example of night hunting.

D.rationale: The day-flying bats contrast with most bats rather than resembling them.

hints: Does the second sentence follow the pattern or break it?
candidates.remember: An exception to a general rule calls for a contrast transition.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Fitzgerald and Wilder. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Fitzgerald won the Booker Prize for Offshore, while Wilder's books became children's classics.
choices.B: Fitzgerald published her first novel in 1977, forty-five years after Wilder published hers.
choices.C: Wilder published Little House in the Big Woods in 1932, when she was 65 years old.
choices.D: Both Fitzgerald and Wilder published their first novels at 60 or older.

candidates.explanation: Only D states something the two writers share: both published a first novel at 60 or older.

A.rationale: This contrasts their achievements rather than stressing what they share.

B.rationale: This emphasizes a difference in timing, not a similarity.

C.rationale: This gives information about Wilder only.

hints: Which choice mentions both writers and something they share?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice for both names and a shared trait.

candidates.remember: A similarity goal needs both subjects and what they have in common.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a method for dating sites, explains its limits, and recommends that archaeologists abandon it.
choices.B: It gives an established date, reports conflicting evidence, and then offers an explanation for the conflict.
choices.C: It compares two forts, describes how each was dated, and concludes that they were built at the same time.
choices.D: It reports a new date for a fort and then gives evidence from pottery that confirms the new date.

candidates.evidence: The team argues that the pottery style must have remained in use for far longer than previously assumed.
candidates.explanation: Sentence 1 gives the old date, sentence 2 gives conflicting radiocarbon evidence, and sentence 3 explains the conflict by proposing that the pottery style lasted longer.

A.rationale: The team does not recommend abandoning pottery dating; it reinterprets how long a style lasted.

D.rationale: The pottery evidence supported the old date; the team explains why it misled.

hints: What does each of the three sentences do?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence's role, then match.

author_checklist.hardness: Choice D reverses the role of the pottery evidence, and choice A overstates the team's conclusion; both catch readers who skim the last sentence.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the historian's claim in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the plague was the main cause of Hollin's decline
choices.B: By arguing that the plague sped up a decline that had already begun for other reasons
choices.C: By denying that the plague had any effect on Hollin's population
choices.D: By questioning whether tax records can show how many people lived in Hollin

candidates.evidence: The plague then sharply reduced a population that was already shrinking.
candidates.explanation: Text 2 dates the decline to about 1310 and the shift of trade downriver, but grants that the plague worsened it. The author would say the plague accelerated an existing decline, not that it caused it.

A.rationale: Text 2 shows the decline began decades before 1349, so the plague was not its starting cause.

C.rationale: Text 2 says the plague "sharply reduced" the population.

D.rationale: Text 2 relies on the tax records rather than doubting them.

hints: When did Hollin's decline begin, according to Text 2?

strategy.explanation: Find what Text 2 says about both the earlier trend and the plague.

candidates.remember: A partial disagreement is often the answer in cross-text items: check what the second text grants.
candidates.revision_note: S019-04 resubmitted unchanged in content and relabelled easy: both blind solvers rated it easy (72%).

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the analyst's claim?

choices.A: Winter ridership rose by 30 percent after the cut, while summer ridership rose by 10 percent.
choices.B: Summer ridership rose by 400 riders after the cut, more than winter ridership rose.
choices.C: After the cut, summer ridership was more than three times winter ridership.
choices.D: Before the cut, average daily ridership in winter was 1,000.

candidates.evidence: in percentage terms, the fare cut increased ridership more in winter than in summer
candidates.explanation: Winter rose 300 on a base of 1,000 (30%); summer rose 400 on a base of 4,000 (10%). Only A gives the percentage comparison the claim needs.

B.rationale: This compares raw numbers, not percentages, and it favors summer, the opposite of the claim.

C.rationale: This compares the seasons with each other, not the size of each season's increase.

D.rationale: A single figure cannot show how much ridership changed.

hints: Does the claim compare raw increases or percentage increases?

strategy.explanation: Note the claim's exact measure before checking the table.

candidates.remember: Match the evidence to the claim's measure: percent change is not raw change.
